questions.q: In the narrowing method taught in this lesson, what should happen right after confirming the symptom?
options: Immediately roll back the most recent deploy
Check the golden signals for the affected service to see which one is driving the symptom
Page every team that owns a downstream dependency
Write the postmortem so it's ready when the incident ends
questions.explain: After confirming the symptom as a measured number, the next step is checking latency, traffic, errors, and saturation to see which signal is actually driving the problem before guessing at a cause.

questions.q: What does the 'Saturation' question in the USE method actually measure?
options: How much electricity the server is drawing
How busy the resource is on a percentage basis
How much work is queued up waiting for the resource
How many errors the resource has logged in the last hour
questions.explain: Saturation measures queued-up demand for a resource, which is distinct from utilization (how busy it is) — a resource can be moderately utilized and still badly saturated.

questions.q: Why does 'check recent changes' belong early in the investigation rather than as a last resort?
options: Because most production incidents trace back to something that changed recently, so ruling it in or out early focuses the rest of the investigation
Because recent changes are always the cause
Because it's the only step that doesn't require dashboard access
Because compliance requires documenting it first
questions.explain: A large share of incidents are triggered by a recent deploy, config change, or flag flip. Checking early either confirms the cause quickly or correctly redirects attention elsewhere, as it did for Northbridge's checkout service.

questions.q: In the Northbridge walkthrough, why was a connection pool at 95% utilization identified as the bottleneck even though errors were low?
options: Because low errors always indicate the true bottleneck
Because its saturation was high — requests were queued waiting for a connection, even though the pool wasn't technically failing
Because the inventory service had a recent deploy
Because checkout's own CPU was maxed out
questions.explain: Utilization alone didn't tell the whole story. High saturation — a long wait queue for connections — identified the pool as undersized for flash-sale load, which is what the USE method is designed to catch.

questions.q: What is the risk of acting on a troubleshooting hypothesis before checking it against data?
options: There is no risk — speed matters more than certainty during an incident
A wrong, unverified hypothesis can turn a short incident into a much longer one by sending the response down the wrong path
It only matters for postmortems, not live incidents
Data always confirms the first hypothesis anyway
questions.explain: Acting on an unverified hunch risks wasted remediation effort and lost time while the real cause goes unaddressed — the method calls for checking a hypothesis against a metric, log, or trace before acting on it.
